title: Rama in the rains
hookLine: Rama's monsoon poem, and why so many Hindu love songs ache
carry: viraha: longing is a kind of love
last: CHATURMAS, THE FOUR HOLY MONTHS OF RAIN.

cards: The smell of wet earth after months of dust. The sky changing color in an afternoon. The whole land seeming to breathe out.

Rama, waiting in the cave, describes the monsoon to Lakshmana, and it's some of the most well-known nature writing in Sanskrit: a long, beautiful, aching poem. Rama sees all of that, and something else too.

teach.b: Here's how Valmiki's Rama sees it. The sky, he says, drank the waters of the sea through the sun's rays, carried them for nine months, and now is giving birth to rain. He sees clouds piled like mountains.
He hears peacocks crying out and sees them dancing. Frogs wake and call. Rivers rush toward the sea.
And the rain that is lovely for everyone is painful for him. Travelers are heading home, he says. Kings have stopped their campaigns.
Everyone is going back to the one they love, and he can't. So every lovely thing he sees, he sees as someone apart from Sita.
That feeling has a name in Sanskrit: viraha, love in separation. And here's why it matters far beyond this cave. Viraha became one of the great roads of Hindu devotion.
In the Bhagavata Purana, when Krishna slips away from the cowherd women of Vrindavan, the gopis search the forest calling for him, and their song of longing is loved to this day.
Saints like Mirabai sang to Krishna as a beloved who felt far away.

teach.h: LONGING IS A KIND OF LOVE.
teach.b: Many teachers read it this way: in bhakti, longing for God isn't a failure of faith. It is love, still working, and the ache keeps the beloved close. That's why so many bhajans sound sad and sweet at once.
Rama in the rains is the same mood from the other side. He doesn't stop loving because Sita is far. He looks harder.
And it meets a life now: anyone missing a grandparent across an ocean, or someone gone. Hindu devotion doesn't say get over it. It says the missing is love.

how: Viraha runs through Hindu devotion: the gopis' longing for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana, Mirabai's songs, and countless bhajans sing of God as a beloved far away. Rama's monsoon description in the Kishkindha Kanda is often cited as an early model for later monsoon poems.

a drought that dries every river in Kishkindha
a flood that Rama must cross to reach the sea

games.q: your nani's favorite bhajan sounds heartbroken over Krishna. by Rama's rain poem, what is that ache?
o: love: longing for God is a way of staying close.
a sign the singer has lost her faith.
just the style of old music.
games.why: viraha: Rama's longing for Sita and the gopis' longing for Krishna are both love, not distance.

practice: Bring to mind someone you miss. Breathe in and let yourself feel it, without fixing it. Breathe out.
If you pray, say softly: Sita Ram, two names many Hindus chant together, the very two this story keeps apart. If you don't, simply say the name of the one you miss.
Let the missing be love, held gently, then come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: The rains. Rama's monsoon poem, and its mood, viraha: love in separation, the ache bhakti songs still sing.

orig.note: Sanskrit viraha: separation, especially the longing of lovers apart. a central mood of Indian love poetry.

carryVoice: Your line: viraha: longing is a kind of love. The missing keeps them close. See you tomorrow.
